title: ‘It is’, and its true nature
theme: It is to be grasped as ‘it is’, and by its true nature — of the two. For one who has grasped it as ‘it is’, its true nature becomes clear.

words.meaning: to be grasped, to be apprehended
words.role: predicate; the self is understood as subject
Śaṅkara: a genitive of selection, «निर्धारणार्था षष्ठी»; Raṅgarāmānuja: ‘by both means’

words.meaning: of the one who has grasped
words.context: Raṅgarāmānuja reads it actively, ‘of the one who has known’, «ज्ञातवतः»
Raṅgarāmānuja: the inner organ, «तत्त्वं भावयति इति तत्त्वभावः - अन्तःकरणम्»

sandhi.type: i + i; i before an unlike vowel; a + u; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: Two like vowels merge into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). i before an unlike vowel becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

samasa.meaning: the being of the reality, its true nature; Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva take bhāva as agent, ‘what makes the reality known’ (see the commentary)

morphology.note: Gerundive of upa + √labh with -tavya, P. 3.1.96 (तव्यत्तव्यानीयरः): ‘to be grasped’.

Past participle upalabdha in the genitive. Raṅgarāmānuja reads the participle actively, ‘of one who has known’, and compares the idiom ‘bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ’ (‘the brahmins have eaten’), «भुक्ता ब्राह्मणाः».
Genitive dual of ubha. Śaṅkara: a genitive of selection, ‘of the two’ (the conditioned and the unconditioned grasping), «निर्धारणार्था षष्ठी»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the two means, scripture and the mind.

translation.literal: As ‘[it] is’ indeed [it] is to be grasped, and by [its] true nature — of the two. For the one grasped as ‘[it] is’, the true nature becomes clear.
translation.readable: It must first be grasped simply as ‘it is’, and then in its true nature. For one who has grasped that it is, its true nature becomes clear.

syntax: The first line has the gerundive upalabdhavyaḥ with two manners, asti ity eva and tattvabhāvena, joined by ca, and the genitive ubhayoḥ, whose relation is disputed. The second line has a genitive of the person (asti ity evopalabdhasya) and the subject tattvabhāvaḥ with prasīdati.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the self’s true nature, free of every adjunct, which ‘becomes clear’, that is, turns towards the knower, «प्रसीदति अभिमुखीभवति». Raṅgarāmānuja: ‘that which makes the reality known’, the inner organ, «तत्त्वं भावयति इति तत्त्वभावः - अन्तःकरणम्», and ‘becomes clear’ means the mind is cleared, «मनः प्रसन्नं भवति, निर्दुष्टं भवति इत्यर्थः». Madhva, in verses he cites, takes it as Viṣṇu, who makes known the nature of matter and souls, «तत्त्वभावस्ततो विष्णुः».

Śaṅkara: of the two ways of grasping, first as ‘it is’ through its adjuncts, then its true nature, «सोपाधिकनिरुपाधिकयोरस्तित्वतत्त्वभावयोः». Raṅgarāmānuja: by the two means, «उभाभ्यां शब्दमनोरूपाभ्याम्», scripture and the mind.

beginner: The previous verse said the self is known only by one who affirms ‘it is’. This verse says that affirmation is a first step. First grasp it simply as ‘it is’; then its true nature becomes clear to you. The commentators read the key word, tattvabhāva, in three ways. Śaṅkara takes it as the self’s true nature: first we know it as the being behind all things, and then its nature beyond all qualities turns towards us. Raṅgarāmānuja takes the same word as ‘the mind’, the faculty that makes reality known: once scripture tells us that God is, and we reflect on it, the mind becomes clear and pure. Madhva, in verses he cites, reads it as a name of Viṣṇu, who makes known the nature of the world and of souls, and by whose grace one knows his greatness.
analogy: First you learn that someone is in the next room; only then, as you go in, do you see who they are.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It is to be grasped as ‘it is’ and by its true nature; for one who has grasped it as ‘it is’, its true nature becomes clear.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: from ‘it is’ to what it truly is
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Rejecting the view that it is not, the self is first to be grasped as ‘it is’ through its adjuncts, «अस्तीत्येव आत्मा उपलब्धव्यः सत्कार्यबुद्ध्याद्युपाधिभिः». Since the effect is nothing apart from the cause, as the Chāndogya says (quoted by him), there is then the self’s true nature without adjuncts. The genitive is one of selection, «निर्धारणार्था षष्ठी»: of the two, for one who first grasped it as ‘it is’, the true nature, free of all adjuncts, becomes clear, «प्रसीदति अभिमुखीभवति».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: scripture, then the clearing mind
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: tattvabhāva is the inner organ, «तत्त्वं भावयति इति तत्त्वभावः - अन्तःकरणम्». The supreme Self is to be grasped as ‘it is’ by it as well: what the Vedānta sentences say is, is to be reflected on and meditated on by the mind too, «मनसाऽपि अस्तीत्येवं मनननिदिध्यासने कर्तव्ये इत्यर्थः». Both means are meant, «उभाभ्यां शब्दमनोरूपाभ्याम्», and for one who has known it so the mind becomes clear, «मनः प्रसन्नं भवति, निर्दुष्टं भवति इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In verses he cites («इति च»), Viṣṇu makes the reality of matter and souls known, «प्रकृतेः पुरुषाणां च तत्त्वं भावयति स्फुटम्», and so is called tattvabhāva, «तत्त्वभावस्ततो विष्णुः»; by his grace his greatness is known.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara’s step from the effect to its cause rests on the Chāndogya’s clay: «वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं मृत्तिकेत्येव सत्यम्».

advaita.text: First grasped as ‘it is’ through its adjuncts, the self then shows its true nature without them, «प्रसीदति अभिमुखीभवति».

visistadvaita.text: What scripture says ‘is’ must also be reflected on and meditated on by the mind, which is then made pure, «मनः प्रसन्नं भवति, निर्दुष्टं भवति इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: tattvabhāva is Viṣṇu, who makes the reality of matter and souls known, «तत्त्वभावस्ततो विष्णुः» (in verses cited by him).

schools.disagreement: The three read tattvabhāva differently: the self’s own true nature (Śaṅkara), the mind that makes reality known (Raṅgarāmānuja), Viṣṇu who makes it known (Madhva). The second line accordingly says that the true nature turns towards the knower, that the mind is cleared, or that by the Lord’s grace his greatness is known.

parallels.note: Quoted by Śaṅkara: the effect is only a name, the clay alone is real.
The preceding verse, whose ‘asti’ this one takes up.

contemporary.text: Much understanding begins with accepting that something is there before one can say what it is. The verse makes that order explicit: first ‘it is’, then its nature. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What did you accept as real before you understood it?
reflect.deeper: Is tattvabhāva what is known, the faculty that knows, or the one who makes it known? What does each reading make the second line say?
reflect.practice: Hold one thing today simply as ‘it is’, without describing it.

flags.note: tattvabhāva as the self’s true nature (Śaṅkara), the inner organ that makes reality known (Raṅgarāmānuja), or Viṣṇu (Madhva, in verses he cites).
